characters: Lekettey: a cheerful nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short hair, wearing a bright green polo shirt, brown shorts, and sandals.
Grandmother: his loving older Ghanaian grandmother wearing a gold-and-green African-print wrapper cloth and matching headscarf.
Shopkeeper: a friendly Ghanaian market stallholder standing beside colourful diamond kites.

narrationPlan.voice: A hopeful boy’s voice for Lekettey; a wise, warm voice for his grandmother
narrationPlan.pace: Warm and steady, with a clear count on page 4 (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light coin-jingle tune with a steady beat (placeholder)
culturalNotes: All cedi amounts in this story are hypothetical (“suppose”) numbers chosen for clear skip-counting in twos.
Many Ghanaian families teach saving with a slotted tin (“susu” box) at home before introducing formal savings accounts with a parent or guardian.
Lekettey’s light Saturday household chores take place safely at home with his grandmother, never as child labour.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?

Confirm that the text clearly frames the prices and rewards as supposed learning numbers.
Confirm that no specific commercial bank or financial product is promoted.

teacherGuide.overview: A practical financial-literacy story teaching the difference between needs and wants, delayed gratification, and skip-counting in twos using hypothetical cedi amounts.
learningGoals: Count in twos to reach a savings target.
Create a simple four-step saving plan for a classroom or personal goal.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics
subjectLinks.link: Skip-counting in twos and simple division

beforeReading: Name four everyday items (water, school shoes, a kite, sweets) and ask learners which are needs and which are wants.
whileReading: Chant the skip-count “Two, four, six, eight, ten!” together on page 4.
afterReading: Draw a simple goal card showing a goal picture, a supposed cost, weekly savings, and number of weeks.
Act out the moment Lekettey chooses his long-term goal over an impulse sweet.
discussion: Why did Lekettey decide not to buy the sweet on page 3?
Why does Grandmother say needs come before wants?
reflection: What is one goal—in learning, sport, or saving—that is worth waiting and working for?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose a storybook costs 12 cedis and you save 3 cedis each week. How many weeks will it take?
Count in twos from 2 to 10. How many pairs of two make 10?

support: Use ten bottle tops arranged in five pairs so learners can touch and count in twos.
stretch: Plan two different weekly saving schedules for a supposed 20-cedi football (for example, 4 cedis vs. 5 cedis a week).

culturalNotes: All cedi amounts in this story are hypothetical (“suppose”) numbers chosen for clear skip-counting in twos.
Many Ghanaian families teach saving with a slotted tin (“susu” box) at home before introducing formal savings accounts with a parent or guardian.
Lekettey’s light Saturday household chores take place safely at home with his grandmother, never as child labour.
localiseThis: Relate the tin to familiar family susu boxes while reminding pupils that real money decisions always involve parents or guardians.
